title: Herodotus, The Histories, Book 3, chapter 89 (Godley translation)
ask_addressed: What ideas, institutions and words passed from Achaemenid and Sasanian Persia to neighbouring and later cultures? State the dated evidence for each strand.
quote: he divided his dominions into twenty provinces, which they call satrapies
summary: Herodotus reports Darius's division of the empire into tributary provinces and gives the Persian term (Greek satrapeie) for them: a dated Greek text naming the institution and the borrowed word.
limits: Fifth-century Greek outsider's account written decades after the events; it records that Greeks knew the system and its name, not that Greek states copied it. Godley's English hides the Greek wording. Verifier: directness lowered from documented to inferred; the passage shows Greeks recording or knowing the Persian term or idea, not a transfer to Greece.

strand.what: satrapy provincial system and the word satrap

title: Herodotus, The Histories, Book 8, chapter 98 (Godley translation): the Persian relay post
ask_addressed: What ideas, institutions and words passed from Achaemenid and Sasanian Persia to neighbouring and later cultures? State the dated evidence for each strand.
quote: This riding-post is called in Persia, angareion.
summary: Herodotus describes the Persian relay-courier system (the source of the later 'neither snow nor rain' motto) and records its Persian name, which Greek adopted as angareion.
limits: Describes the system in the context of 480 BCE; it does not say Greece or later states adopted it. Persian origin of the word is stated here, its later spread is not. Verifier: directness lowered from documented to inferred; the passage shows Greeks recording or knowing the Persian term or idea, not a transfer to Greece.

title: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book I, Prologue (Hicks translation, with notes)
ask_addressed: What ideas, institutions and words passed from Achaemenid and Sasanian Persia to neighbouring and later cultures? State the dated evidence for each strand.
quote: according to the Magi men will live in a future life and be immortal
summary: Reports (citing Theopompus, 4th c. BCE, Hermippus, Eudoxus) that Magi taught two principles, Oromasdes and Arimanius, and a future life: the Greek-side attestation that Persian dualism and afterlife ideas were known in Greece.
limits: Third-century CE compiler quoting lost earlier authors; Hicks's footnote notes the Theopompus passage is read as Zoroastrian doctrine by Moulton but the wording is ambiguous. Shows Greek knowledge only; says nothing about Judaism. Verifier: directness lowered from documented to inferred; the passage shows Greeks recording or knowing the Persian term or idea, not a transfer to Greece.

strand.what: dualist principles and a future life taught by the Magi

title: Josephus, Antiquities of the Jews, Book 11, chapter 1 (Whiston translation)
ask_addressed: What ideas, institutions and words passed from Achaemenid and Sasanian Persia to neighbouring and later cultures? State the dated evidence for each strand.
quote: send back my people to their own land, and build my temple
summary: Josephus says Cyrus read Isaiah's prophecy and released the Jews from Babylon to rebuild the Temple: an ancient Jewish statement that Persian imperial policy enabled the restoration.
limits: Written c. 1st c. CE, about 600 years after the events, with a theological framing. Compare the Cyrus Cylinder candidate.

strand.what: royal permission for return and Temple rebuilding

title: Cyrus Cylinder (Wikipedia pointer to the scholarly dispute over its Jewish relevance)
ask_addressed: What ideas, institutions and words passed from Achaemenid and Sasanian Persia to neighbouring and later cultures? State the dated evidence for each strand.
quote: This interpretation has been disputed, as the text identifies only Mesopotamian sanctuaries, and makes no mention of Jews, Jerusalem, or Judea.
summary: The article reports that the Babylonian cylinder is traditionally read as backing a repatriation policy for Jews but that specialists dispute this, and it places the text within older Mesopotamian royal-inscription tradition.
limits: Wikipedia is a pointer only; the underlying scholarship (Kuhrt and others, per the article) was not opened. The page does not deny a Judean return, only that the cylinder documents it.

strand.what: a Cyrus policy of repatriating exiles

title: Paradise (Wikipedia pointer: Old Iranian pairidaeza into Hebrew pardes and Greek paradeisos)
ask_addressed: What ideas, institutions and words passed from Achaemenid and Sasanian Persia to neighbouring and later cultures? State the dated evidence for each strand.
quote: The Hebrew word pardes appears only in the post-Exilic period (after 538 BCE)
summary: The article gives the Old Iranian origin of the word, its borrowing into Greek (Xenophon, Anabasis, early 4th c. BCE) and Hebrew (Song of Songs, Ecclesiastes, Nehemiah). A loanword strand with dated attestations, here at the pointer level.
limits: Wikipedia is a pointer; the etymological sources it cites were not opened. A word entering Hebrew shows contact, not transfer of doctrine. Xenophon's Greek text (Perseus 1999.01.0201, 1.2.7) shows the Greek use but does not itself state the Iranian origin.

strand.what: pardes (garden, park) from Old Iranian pairidaeza

title: Zoroastrianism (Wikipedia pointer: Mary Boyce on borrowing by Judaism, Christianity and Islam)
ask_addressed: What do sceptical specialists say about how far Zoroastrianism shaped Judaism and Christianity, and about Persian administrative models?
quote: These doctrines were to become familiar articles of faith to much of mankind, through borrowing by Judaism, Christianity and Islam
summary: The article quotes Mary Boyce's strong-influence position: individual judgement, heaven and hell, bodily resurrection and last judgement taught first by Zoroaster and later borrowed.
limits: Secondhand quotation on Wikipedia; Boyce's original was not opened. It asserts rather than demonstrates a route and relies on later Zoroastrian texts for the doctrines' early form. Verifier: the quoted Boyce passage covers judgement, heaven and hell, resurrection and last judgement; angels and demons come from the article's separate list of parallels, not from this quote.

strand.what: resurrection, final judgement, heaven and hell, angels and demons

title: Zoroastrianism (Wikipedia pointer: scholars who diminish or reject influence on Judaism)
ask_addressed: What do sceptical specialists say about how far Zoroastrianism shaped Judaism and Christianity, and about Persian administrative models?
quote: Other scholars diminish or reject such influences, noting that "Zoroastrianism has a unique theistic doctrine which combines dualism, polytheism and pantheism"
summary: The same article lists the parallels proponents cite, then records scholars who diminish or reject influence, say there is little concrete evidence on Zoroastrianism's origin and development, and cite Lester Grabbe's framing of what is Iranian as against Greek.
limits: Wikipedia pointer; the named scholars were not opened (the page ties the quotation to unopened sources). The page itself shows the question is disputed rather than settled either way.

title: The Seleukid Royal Economy: the finances and financial administration of the Seleukid empire (PhD thesis, UCL)
venue: UCL Discovery (University of London PhD thesis)
ask_addressed: What do sceptical specialists say about how far Zoroastrianism shaped Judaism and Christianity, and about Persian administrative models?
quote: the financial administration of the empire owed much to Achaemenid prototypes.
summary: The abstract concludes that regional and district officials responsible for satrapal finances and royal land, reporting to the king, show Achaemenid precedent in Seleukid administration (Hellenistic inheritance of Persian administrative models).
limits: Doctoral thesis; opened the abstract and passages located by search, not the whole 800k-character text. Inference from administrative parallels and epigraphy, not a statement that Seleukids deliberately copied a Persian model. Verifier: kind changed from primary to secondary (a modern thesis); quote is in the abstract (page 2).

strand.what: satrapal financial administration and district officials

title: After the Achaemenids: exchange, transmission and transformation in the visual culture of Babylonia, Iran and Bactria c.330 - c.100 BC (DPhil thesis, Oxford)
venue: Oxford Research Archive (University of Oxford DPhil thesis)
ask_addressed: What do sceptical specialists say about how far Zoroastrianism shaped Judaism and Christianity, and about Persian administrative models?
quote: While this approach brings many benefits, most scholars call for a less extreme interpretation.
summary: The literature review describes the Kuhrt/Sherwin-White emphasis on Achaemenid continuity in Seleukid history and says most scholars want a less extreme version, with Briant's 'last of the Achaemenids' useful for administration but not to be stretched to kingship.
limits: A review of historiography within an art-history thesis, not an administrative study; it signals the sceptical consensus on overstating Persian continuity, and notes the Achaemenid legacy mattered to Armenian rulers and Antiochus I of Commagene.

title: Oman and late Sasanian imperialism
venue: Arabian Archaeology and Epigraphy 28, pp. 264-284 (White Rose accepted version)
discipline: Late antique and early Islamic history
ask_addressed: What ideas, institutions and words passed from Achaemenid and Sasanian Persia to neighbouring and later cultures? State the dated evidence for each strand.
quote: Arguments about the nature of late Sasanian imperial involvement in Oman have become quite polarised over the past few decades.
summary: Argues that later Arabic literary sources, read with other evidence, indicate Sasanian involvement in south-east Arabia not far from what many archaeologists conclude, while noting the evidence is split between historians and archaeologists.
limits: Concerns Sasanian presence and administration in Oman, not ideas passed to Islam directly; the sources are largely Muslim-era retrospectives, so the extent of the Sasanian legacy there is contested.

strand.what: imperial administration and presence in south-east Arabia

title: Graeco-Arabic translation movement (Wikipedia pointer: Pahlavi texts in the Abbasid translation movement)
ask_addressed: What ideas, institutions and words passed from Achaemenid and Sasanian Persia to neighbouring and later cultures? State the dated evidence for each strand.
quote: texts from many other languages such as Pahlavi, Sanskrit, and Syriac were also translated into Arabic
summary: The article states that Middle Persian (Pahlavi) texts were translated into Arabic alongside Greek ones in the Abbasid movement and links the movement to the House of Wisdom and the Sasanian foundation of Gondishapur.
limits: Wikipedia pointer; the Gutas book it relates to (Greek Thought, Arabic Culture) could not be opened here (archive.org full text blocked). The page treats Greek as the movement's main focus; Pahlavi's weight is not quantified.

title: Barmakids (Wikipedia pointer: Irano-Islamic secretaries and the Abbasid diwan al-kharaj)
ask_addressed: What ideas, institutions and words passed from Achaemenid and Sasanian Persia to neighbouring and later cultures? State the dated evidence for each strand.
quote: the Irano-Islamic class of secretaries (kuttab in Arabic, dabiran in Persian), was formed
summary: The article says that under the Abbasids Khalid al-Barmaki headed the finance department and that an Irano-Islamic scribal class (kuttab, from Persian dabiran) arose in its offices: a pointer for Persian administrative personnel and practice in the early Abbasid state.
limits: Wikipedia pointer; the underlying sources were not opened. The page describes an Iranian family and class in Abbasid administration, not a documented copying of Sasanian procedures.

title: Barmakids (Wikipedia pointer: quoted scholarly caution on the Khurasan route of learning to the caliphate)
venue: Wikipedia (blockquote; author not named in the text read)
ask_addressed: What ideas, institutions and words passed from Achaemenid and Sasanian Persia to neighbouring and later cultures? State the dated evidence for each strand.
quote: Khurāsān and Transoxiana were effectively bypassed in this transfer of learning from India to Islam
summary: A scholar quoted on the page argues that Barmakid patronage of translation happened at the Iraqi caliphal court, so the eastern Persian provinces were not the channel for Indian learning, a caution against crediting Iranian lands with the transfer.
limits: Wikipedia pointer; the quoted scholar and work were not opened or identified from the page text. It concerns Indian medical texts, so it limits one Persian-mediation claim rather than all of them. Verifier: the page's footnote attributes the blockquote to Bosworth and Asimov, History of Civilizations of Central Asia vol. 4 part 2, p. 300; not opened.

title: Persian language (Wikipedia pointer: Persian as a bureaucratic and literary language in Ottoman and Indian courts)
ask_addressed: What ideas, institutions and words passed from Achaemenid and Sasanian Persia to neighbouring and later cultures? State the dated evidence for each strand.
quote: used officially as a language of bureaucracy even by non-native speakers, such as the Ottomans in Anatolia, the Delhi Sultanates and Mughals
summary: The lead states that Persian was an official bureaucratic language under the Ottomans and the Delhi and Mughal courts and influenced Turkic, Armenian, Georgian, Greek and Indo-Aryan languages (the loanword route into Ottoman Turkish and Urdu).
limits: Wikipedia pointer; no loanword counts or dated first attestations were opened. Swahili: no source opened (gap).

strand.what: Persian as administrative language and source of loanwords
